expectations.text: Takes the event's published policy, response-team composition and reporting channels as given rather than rewriting or reinterpreting them
expectations.evidence: Some points support this. The response team is kept as given ('Five trained response-team members wear [badge / lanyard colour]', 'You are not the response team, and you don't investigate'). The reporting email is left as a placeholder. The organizer is told to 'Make sure the CoC steps and channels match your published policy exactly.' Other points go against it. The response writes its own five-step CoC procedure and adds it to the brief unasked ('One addition to your brief'). Without any source, it says 'The skill treats this as non-negotiable.' expectations.text: Takes the event's published policy, response-team composition and reporting channels as given rather than rewriting or reinterpreting them
expectations.evidence: The briefing does not cite or defer to an event code of conduct, a named response team or official reporting channels. It invents its own: a radio call 'CoC, [location]', 'send the person to a CoC badge holder', and 'The code-of-conduct team takes it from there'. It also sets a rule that volunteers must not handle reports. Other details use [bracket] placeholders, but this escalation path is written as fixed text. The note admits the line was added and suggests swapping in the team's call sign or email. Even so, the draft prints a made-up channel and team instead of pointing to the event's pub
